title: Who pays
hook: adult Muslims with wealth above the threshold for a full lunar year

segments.voice: Yesterday, zakat, the word that means to purify and to grow, and your line: giving makes it grow. Did you give the thing you chose? Did anything feel lighter? Day one thousand ninety-four.

Mu'adh ibn Jabal is packing for Yemen. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is sending him there to teach, and before he leaves, he gets his instructions, step by step, in the order he's to give them. The report is in Sahih al-Bukhari. First, call the people to the testimony. If they accept that, teach them the prayers. And if they accept that, tell them Allah has made a charity obligatory on them, taken from their rich and given back to their poor. From their rich. To their poor. In a handful of words, the answer to a question that sounds simple and isn't: who actually pays zakat? Today, who pays.
screen: `MU'ADH, PACKING FOR YEMEN.` → `TESTIMONY, THEN PRAYER, THEN ZAKAT.` → `FROM THEIR RICH, TO THEIR POOR.`

segments.voice: First, it's a duty for Muslims. The Qur'an sets it right beside the prayer. In surah two, in Pickthall's words: "Establish worship, pay the poor-due, and bow your heads with those who bow." Worship and the poor-due, in one breath. Zakat is part of the practice of Islam, so it's asked of Muslims, not of their neighbors. Second, it's asked of the rich, in the Prophet's sense. Not a millionaire. Someone whose wealth passes a set line, the threshold, which gets its own day tomorrow. Below that line, nothing is owed. A person who barely has enough is one of the people zakat is meant to reach, not one of the people it's taken from. Third, the wealth has to sit. A hadith in the Sunan of Abu Dawud says no zakat is due on wealth until a year has passed over it. Money that comes in and goes straight back out to rent and groceries isn't what's counted. What's counted is what stays. That's why your line says a share once a year. It's a yearly reckoning, not a toll on every paycheck. Fourth, the hard edge: who counts as an adult owner? Here the schools of law differ, and say so plainly. On savings held by a child, the Hanafi school says no zakat is due. Other schools say it is due, and a guardian pays it from the child's wealth. Shia jurists have their own rulings again. Nobody here is ranked; each answer comes with its own reasons. Put together, the picture is narrower than people sometimes assume. Not everyone pays. Not every dollar. A Muslim, past the line, on wealth that stayed a year, gives a share, once a year.
screen: `A DUTY OF MUSLIMS.` · `ON THOSE PAST THE LINE.` · `ON WEALTH THAT STAYED A YEAR.` · `WHO COUNTS AS THE OWNER?` · then, large: `ESTABLISH WORSHIP, PAY THE POOR-DUE.`

segments.voice: The practice: check if you qualify, or, if zakat isn't part of your life, check what you're holding onto. Settle, and breathe. Without opening any app, ask yourself three questions. Is there money that has stayed with me, untouched, for a long while? Roughly how much? And is it more than I need to live on? If you're Muslim, those questions are the start of working out your zakat. If not, they're still a quiet way to see what you've been keeping. Just notice the answers. No judgment. The bell holds the time.
Who pays. A Muslim whose wealth is past the threshold and has stayed a year. Taken from the rich, given to the poor. Today's word.
Your line: a share once a year. Today, notice one thing you own that has just been sitting, and ask what it's for. Tomorrow: the threshold, the line itself. Day one thousand ninety-four.

howItsDone: Muslims whose savings pass the threshold and have been held a year work out their zakat once a year, and those unsure of their school's rules, for example on a child's savings, ask a scholar or a zakat body.

fork.setup: you're Mu'adh, arriving in Yemen. the people have accepted the testimony and the prayers. what are you told to teach them next?
options: that they must send their wealth to Medina.
that a charity is due, taken from their rich and given to their poor.
fork.reveal: a charity taken from their rich and given back to their poor. it starts and ends among the people themselves.

trapdoor: what you thought: all Muslims pay zakat on everything they earn.
what it means: a Muslim past the threshold pays a share, once a year, on wealth that stayed.
what a scholar hears: the schools differ on who counts as the owner, as with a child's savings, and each gives its reasons.
recall: odd, an odd number of units

notes: Pickthall 2:43 quoted from memory; his text continues '(in worship)' after 'who bow'. Confirm wording.
Bukhari 1395 (Mu'adh sent to Yemen): confirm number; the same hadith also appears as Bukhari 1458 and 1496 in some numberings.
Abu Dawud 1573 (no zakat until a year passes): confirm number and grading.
Children's wealth: Hanafi no; Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali yes via guardian. Confirm, and confirm the Ja'fari position is fairly summarized only as 'their own rulings'.
Index hook names 'a full lunar year'; the lunar year is left for day 1097 (hawl).
Conditions such as freedom and full ownership are left out to keep one idea; a Keeper may add them.
Editor: 'the other Sunni schools' softened to 'other schools' (claims rule: no all-schools claim beyond the cited texts).
